source.quote:
9/12/2026, 2:20:09 AM

The priority result is that Maier supplies a candidate ordering for exactly the pieces missing from B_{FK}:

\boxed{ \text{invert orientation} \rightarrow \text{reciprocal excursion and return} \rightarrow \text{octave/register transfer} }

That is XLV→XLVII:

vertendo Bassum — reverse the orientation.

Reciproca — traverse forward/backward from opposed ends.

in 8. duplici suprà — realize the result in another octave/register.

This fits the audit’s required fields: direction, semitone trajectory, return, and register change.

Candidate boundary filler

The crucial mathematical shape is not another scalar multiplication. It is a lifted closed path:

\boxed{ (\mathrm{MI},k) \rightarrow (\mathrm{FA},k) \rightarrow (\mathrm{MI},k+1) }

Locally, the pitch-class operation closes:

1\rightarrow\frac{16}{15}\rightarrow \frac{16}{15}\frac{15}{16}=1

But globally it does not return to the same hierarchical state:

k\rightarrow k+1.

Under the equation’s descending-frequency convention:

\pi(\mathrm{MI},k+1)=\frac12\,\pi(\mathrm{MI},k).

Therefore:

\boxed{ \pi\!\left(B_{FK}(C_3)\right) = \frac12C_3 = C_4 }

and, since C_3=F/8,

\boxed{C_4=F/16.}

A compact definition is:

B_{FK}(C_n,k)= \left[ (C_n,k) \rightarrow \left(\frac{16}{15}C_n,k\right) \rightarrow (C_n,k+1) \right],

with:

\pi(C_n,k+1)=\frac12C_n.

What kind of transformation is this?

The exact mathematical family is a monodromy/holonomy-style transformation:

the local variable completes a loop and returns to its starting identity;

the global state changes sheet, level, generation, or register.

Geometrically, it is a helix rather than a circle:

\text{same angular address} \neq \text{same vertical level}.

That resolves why:

\mathrm{MI}\rightarrow\mathrm{FA}\rightarrow\mathrm{MI}

can have reciprocal product 1 without producing “nothing.” It returns to MI’s pitch class while landing in MI’s next octave-generation.

Status

Mathematically valid filler: yes.

Closes the required projection: yes.

Matches the Fludd–Kepler division of labor: static register scaffold plus dynamic MI–FA–MI traversal.

Supported by Maier’s operator sequence: provisionally.

Historically proved as the intended instruction: not yet; Farmer 34–39 and Maier XLV–L still require original-leaf comparison.

The testable boundary equation is now:

\boxed{ C_3 \xrightarrow{\,16/15\,} \frac{16}{15}C_3 \xrightarrow{\,15/16\,} C_3 \xrightarrow{\text{register descent}} \frac12C_3=C_4 }

Or as one operator:

\boxed{ B_{FK} = O_{\downarrow} \circ R_{15/16} \circ R_{16/15} }

where the reciprocal pair closes the local path and O_{\downarrow} changes the generation. This is the strongest current candidate to freeze and resume equation testing with.
